scenario: A $3.0\text{ kg}$ block is released from rest on a rough incline that makes $30^\circ$ with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between block and incline is $\mu_k = 0.20$. Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Draw a free-body diagram of the block and label each force.
parts.modelResponse: Three forces: weight $mg$ straight down from the centre; normal force $F_N$ perpendicular to the incline surface, away from it; kinetic friction $f_k$ along the surface, directed **up** the slope (the block slides down, so friction opposes that).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the normal force on the block.
parts.modelResponse: Perpendicular axis (no perpendicular acceleration): $F_N = mg\cos 30^\circ = (3.0)(10)(0.866) = 26\text{ N}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the block's acceleration down the incline.
parts.modelResponse: $f_k = \mu_k F_N = (0.20)(26) = 5.2\text{ N}$. Along the slope (down-slope positive): $ma = mg\sin 30^\circ - f_k = (3.0)(10)(0.5) - 5.2 = 15 - 5.2 = 9.8\text{ N}$, so $a = 9.8/3.0 = 3.3\text{ m/s}^2$ down the slope. (Or $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) = 10(0.5 - 0.173) = 3.3\text{ m/s}^2$.)

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The incline is made steeper. State, with reasoning, what happens to the normal force and to the acceleration.
parts.modelResponse: Steeper $\theta$: $\cos\theta$ decreases, so $F_N = mg\cos\theta$ **decreases**. $\sin\theta$ increases and the friction term $\mu_k\cos\theta$ decreases, so $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$ **increases**.

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt three correct forces, 1 pt friction up-slope with justification. (b) 1 pt $F_N = mg\cos\theta$, 1 pt $26\text{ N}$. (c) 1 pt $f_k = \mu_k F_N$, 1 pt correct signed sum along the slope, 1 pt $a \approx 3.3\text{ m/s}^2$ down. (d) 1 pt $F_N$ decreases (because $\cos\theta$ falls), 1 pt $a$ increases.

scenario: A student wants to measure the coefficient of static friction $\mu_s$ between a wooden block and a wooden board, using only the board, the block, a protractor, and a way to prop the board at various angles.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe a procedure that would let the student determine $\mu_s$.
parts.modelResponse: Place the block on the board and slowly raise one end, increasing the angle. Record the angle $\theta_c$ at which the block *just* begins to slide. Repeat several times (re-setting the block) and average $\theta_c$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Derive the relationship between $\mu_s$ and the measured critical angle $\theta_c$.
parts.modelResponse: At the verge of sliding, the down-slope weight component equals the maximum static friction: $mg\sin\theta_c = \mu_s F_N = \mu_s mg\cos\theta_c$. Divide by $mg\cos\theta_c$: $\mu_s = \tan\theta_c$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The student worries that a heavier block will give a different result. Explain whether the mass of the block affects the measurement.
parts.modelResponse: It does not. Both $mg\sin\theta_c$ and $\mu_s mg\cos\theta_c$ scale with $m$, so $m$ cancels: $\mu_s = \tan\theta_c$ is independent of the block's mass.

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt tilt until it just slips, 1 pt record that angle, 1 pt repeat/average. (b) 1 pt sets $mg\sin\theta_c = \mu_s mg\cos\theta_c$, 1 pt divides correctly, 1 pt $\mu_s = \tan\theta_c$. (c) 1 pt states mass-independent, 1 pt shows $m$ cancels.

scenario: A $1000\text{ kg}$ car rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius $50\text{ m}$ at a constant $15\text{ m/s}$. Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Draw a free-body diagram of the car as seen from behind, and identify which force provides the centripetal acceleration.
parts.modelResponse: Gravity $mg$ down, normal force $F_N$ up (equal, cancelling), and static friction $f_s$ horizontal, pointing toward the centre of the curve. Static friction is the force that provides the centripetal acceleration; there is no separate 'centripetal force'.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the friction force.
parts.modelResponse: $f_s = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{(1000)(15)^2}{50} = \dfrac{225000}{50} = 4500\text{ N}$, directed toward the centre.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The coefficient of static friction is $\mu_s = 0.60$. Find the maximum speed for this curve, and state what happens if the car exceeds it.
parts.modelResponse: $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r} = \sqrt{(0.60)(10)(50)} = \sqrt{300} \approx 17\text{ m/s}$. Above this speed the required $mv^2/r$ exceeds the maximum friction $\mu_s mg$, so friction cannot bend the path tightly enough and the car slides toward the outside of the curve.

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt correct real forces (no centripetal-force arrow), 1 pt names friction as centripetal. (b) 1 pt $f_s = mv^2/r$, 1 pt $4500\text{ N}$. (c) 1 pt $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$, 1 pt $\approx 17\text{ m/s}$, 1 pt slides toward the outside.

scenario: A ball of mass $0.30\text{ kg}$ is swung in a vertical circle of radius $0.80\text{ m}$ on a string. Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: At the top of the circle the ball moves at $4.0\text{ m/s}$. Find the string tension there.
parts.modelResponse: At the top, 'toward the centre' is downward; the real downward forces are tension and gravity: $F_T + mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. So $F_T = \dfrac{(0.30)(4.0)^2}{0.80} - (0.30)(10) = \dfrac{4.8}{0.80} - 3.0 = 6.0 - 3.0 = 3.0\text{ N}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the minimum speed at the top for which the string stays taut.
parts.modelResponse: The string goes slack when $F_T = 0$: $mg = \dfrac{mv_{\min}^2}{r} \Rightarrow v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{(10)(0.80)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.8\text{ m/s}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A student says the ball 'feels an outward force at the top that the string has to fight'. Correct this statement.
parts.modelResponse: There is no outward force. At the top the ball is accelerating *downward* (toward the centre), and the real forces — gravity and tension — both point that way. The ball's tendency to continue in a straight line is inertia, not a force. The string pulls the ball *inward*, adding to gravity to give the needed $mv^2/r$.

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt $F_T + mg = mv^2/r$ (both forces inward at the top), 1 pt correct substitution, 1 pt $3.0\text{ N}$. (b) 1 pt sets $F_T = 0$, 1 pt $v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$, 1 pt $\approx 2.8\text{ m/s}$. (c) 1 pt no outward force / net force is inward, 1 pt identifies inertia (straight-line tendency), not a force.

scenario:
A spring is loaded with hanging weights and the stretch from natural length is recorded:

| Force (N) | Stretch (m) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0 |
| 1.0 | 0.020 |
| 2.0 | 0.040 |
| 3.0 | 0.058 |
| 4.0 | 0.082 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the shape of a graph of force (y) against stretch (x), and identify the region where Hooke's law applies.
parts.modelResponse: For the first three points the graph is a straight line through the origin — Hooke's law applies there. Beyond about $3.0\text{ N}$ the line begins to curve (the $4.0\text{ N}$ point sits above the straight-line trend), so the spring is past its elastic limit and Hooke's law no longer applies.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Determine the spring constant from the linear region.
parts.modelResponse: Slope of the straight part: $k = \dfrac{\Delta F}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{2.0 - 0}{0.040 - 0} = 50\text{ N/m}$ (the $1.0/0.020$ pair gives the same value).

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Predict the stretch for a $2.5\text{ N}$ load, and state the assumption you are making.
parts.modelResponse: $x = F/k = 2.5/50 = 0.050\text{ m}$. Assumption: $2.5\text{ N}$ is still within the linear (Hooke's-law) region, which it is — it is below the $\sim 3.0\text{ N}$ where the graph starts to bend.

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt straight line through origin for small loads, 1 pt identifies deviation beyond $\sim 3\text{ N}$, 1 pt links to elastic limit / Hooke's law breaking down. (b) 1 pt slope method on the linear part, 1 pt $k = 50\text{ N/m}$. (c) 1 pt $x = F/k = 0.050\text{ m}$, 1 pt states the linear-range assumption.

scenario: A $50\text{ kg}$ student stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator. Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: What does the scale read when the elevator is at rest?

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The elevator accelerates upward at $2.0\text{ m/s}^2$. Draw a free-body diagram of the student and find the scale reading.
parts.modelResponse: Forces on the student: normal force $F_N$ up, gravity $mg$ down; net force is upward. $F_N - mg = ma \Rightarrow F_N = m(g + a) = 50(10 + 2.0) = 600\text{ N}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The elevator cable then breaks and the elevator falls freely. What does the scale read, and why?
parts.modelResponse: $a = -g$ (free fall). $F_N = m(g + a) = m(g - g) = 0\text{ N}$. The student and the scale fall together with the same acceleration, so the scale surface exerts no force on the student — apparent weightlessness. Gravity is still acting; there is just no contact force.

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt $500\text{ N}$. (b) 1 pt FBD (normal up, gravity down, net up), 1 pt $F_N = m(g+a)$, 1 pt $600\text{ N}$. (c) 1 pt $0\text{ N}$, 1 pt $a = -g$ so $F_N = 0$, 1 pt explains that gravity still acts / it is the contact force that vanishes.

scenario: On a frictionless table, a $4.0\text{ kg}$ block is connected by a light string over an ideal pulley at the table's edge to a $2.0\text{ kg}$ block that hangs. The system is released from rest. Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Draw a free-body diagram for each block.
parts.modelResponse: Table block: gravity down, normal force up (cancel), string tension $F_T$ horizontal toward the pulley. Hanging block: string tension $F_T$ up, gravity $m_2 g$ down (gravity is larger, so it accelerates down).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the acceleration of the system.
parts.modelResponse: Treat both blocks as one system. The only external force along the motion is the weight of the hanging block, $m_2 g = 20\text{ N}$; the total mass is $6.0\text{ kg}$. $a = \dfrac{m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{20}{6.0} = 3.3\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the string tension.
parts.modelResponse: Isolate the table block: the only horizontal force is $F_T$, so $F_T = m_1 a = (4.0)(3.3) = 13\text{ N}$. (Check with the hanging block: $m_2 g - F_T = 20 - 13 = 7 = m_2 a = (2.0)(3.3) \approx 6.7$. ✓)

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why the tension is less than the weight of the hanging block.
parts.modelResponse: The hanging block is accelerating **downward**, so the net force on it must be downward: $m_2 g - F_T = m_2 a > 0$, which requires $F_T < m_2 g$. If the tension equalled the weight, the hanging block would not accelerate at all.

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt table-block FBD, 1 pt hanging-block FBD (tension up, weight down). (b) 1 pt system approach with external force $= m_2 g$, 1 pt total mass $6.0\text{ kg}$, 1 pt $a \approx 3.3\text{ m/s}^2$. (c) 1 pt isolates one block, 1 pt $F_T \approx 13\text{ N}$. (d) 1 pt net force on the hanging block is downward, 1 pt therefore $F_T < m_2 g$.

scenario:
Two blocks, $A$ ($1.0\text{ kg}$) and $B$ ($2.0\text{ kg}$), sit in contact on a frictionless floor. A horizontal force of $9.0\text{ N}$ is applied to block $A$, pushing both blocks. A student writes:

'The force on block $B$ is $9.0\text{ N}$, so its acceleration is $a_B = 9.0/2.0 = 4.5\text{ m/s}^2$.'

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Identify the student's error.
parts.modelResponse: The student assumed the full $9.0\text{ N}$ applied force acts on block $B$. It does not — the applied force acts on $A$. What acts on $B$ is only the contact force from $A$, which is smaller.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the correct acceleration of the two-block system.
parts.modelResponse: Both blocks move together: $a = \dfrac{F}{m_A + m_B} = \dfrac{9.0}{3.0} = 3.0\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the contact force between $A$ and $B$.
parts.modelResponse: Isolate block $B$: the only horizontal force on it is the contact push from $A$. $F_{contact} = m_B a = (2.0)(3.0) = 6.0\text{ N}$. (Check on $A$: $9.0 - 6.0 = 3.0 = m_A a = (1.0)(3.0)$. ✓)

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt the applied force acts on $A$, not $B$, 1 pt $B$ only feels the (smaller) contact force. (b) 1 pt system mass $3.0\text{ kg}$, 1 pt $a = 3.0\text{ m/s}^2$. (c) 1 pt isolates $B$, 1 pt $F_{contact} = m_B a$, 1 pt $6.0\text{ N}$.

lesson: Newton's Third Law: Interaction Pairs vs Balanced Forces
scenario: A large truck (mass $8000\text{ kg}$) and a small car (mass $1200\text{ kg}$) collide head-on. During the collision the truck exerts a force on the car and the car exerts a force on the truck.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Compare the magnitudes of the two forces during the collision, and name the principle.
parts.modelResponse: The two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction at every instant of contact — Newton's third law. This holds regardless of the vehicles' masses or speeds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compare the magnitudes of the two accelerations during the collision.
parts.modelResponse: The car's acceleration is much larger. Since $a = F/m$ and the forces are equal, the vehicle with the smaller mass (the car, $1200\text{ kg}$) has the larger acceleration — about $8000/1200 \approx 6.7$ times the truck's.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: In one short paragraph, explain to someone who thinks 'the truck hits the car harder' why that is not what Newton's third law says, and what *is* true about the collision.
parts.modelResponse: The interaction force is a single mutual push: the truck-on-car and car-on-truck forces are exactly equal in size, so neither 'hits harder'. What differs is the *effect* of that equal force. Because the car has far less mass, the same force produces a much greater acceleration — and hence a much greater change in velocity and far more damage — for the car than for the truck. 'The truck wins' describes the outcome (accelerations, injuries), not the forces.

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt equal and opposite, 1 pt names Newton's third law / notes mass-independence. (b) 1 pt car's acceleration larger, 1 pt because $a = F/m$ with equal $F$ and smaller $m$. (c) 1 pt forces are equal (no one hits harder), 1 pt equal force → unequal acceleration because of unequal mass, 1 pt connects to the greater velocity change / damage for the car.

scenario: A $6.0\text{ kg}$ crate is pulled across a level floor by a rope at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal with a tension of $40\text{ N}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between crate and floor is $\mu_k = 0.25$. Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 30^\circ = 0.50$, $\cos 30^\circ = 0.87$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Draw a free-body diagram of the crate and choose axes.
parts.modelResponse: Forces: weight $mg$ down, normal force $F_N$ up, rope tension $40\text{ N}$ at $30^\circ$ above horizontal (components: $34.8\text{ N}$ horizontal, $20\text{ N}$ vertical up), kinetic friction $f_k$ backward along the floor. Axes: horizontal ($x$, direction of motion) and vertical ($y$).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the normal force.
parts.modelResponse: Vertical equilibrium (no vertical acceleration): $F_N + T\sin 30^\circ - mg = 0 \Rightarrow F_N = mg - T\sin 30^\circ = (6.0)(10) - (40)(0.50) = 60 - 20 = 40\text{ N}$. (Note $F_N < mg$: the rope lifts part of the weight.)

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the crate's acceleration.
parts.modelResponse: $f_k = \mu_k F_N = (0.25)(40) = 10\text{ N}$. Horizontal: $ma = T\cos 30^\circ - f_k = (40)(0.87) - 10 = 34.8 - 10 = 24.8\text{ N}$, so $a = 24.8/6.0 = 4.1\text{ m/s}^2$ in the direction of motion.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: If the rope were instead horizontal (same $40\text{ N}$), would the acceleration be larger or smaller? Explain without a full recalculation.
parts.modelResponse: The full $40\text{ N}$ would then act horizontally (larger driving component, $40$ vs $34.8\text{ N}$), **but** $F_N$ would rise to $mg = 60\text{ N}$, so friction would rise to $\mu_k(60) = 15\text{ N}$. Driving force up by $5.2\text{ N}$, friction up by $5\text{ N}$ — nearly a wash. A quick calc: $a = (40 - 15)/6.0 = 4.2\text{ m/s}^2$, essentially the same. So raising the angle from horizontal barely changes $a$ here; there is an optimal small angle that does a little better.

scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt all four forces with the rope resolved, 1 pt horizontal/vertical axes. (b) 1 pt $\sum F_y = 0$ including $T\sin\theta$, 1 pt $F_N = mg - T\sin\theta$, 1 pt $40\text{ N}$. (c) 1 pt $f_k = \mu_k F_N$ with the reduced $F_N$, 1 pt horizontal $\sum F = T\cos\theta - f_k$, 1 pt $a \approx 4.1\text{ m/s}^2$. (d) 1 pt notes both the larger horizontal component AND the larger $F_N$/friction, 1 pt concludes roughly unchanged (accept 'slightly larger' with sound reasoning).
